extracted.intended_audience: college trustees, presidents, faculty, and higher-education administrators involved in hiring
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for selecting college and university officers (presidents, professors, tutors) and for organizing appointment procedures to promote institutional efficiency and harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for a college president
rubrics_metrics.description: The college president must have tact; executive capacity and force; be business-like in methods; command the confidence and respect of trustees, teachers, students, alumni, and the community; be a good judge of men; and have training (usually from experience). He must have public confidence to attract support; be in harmony with the faculty; and must be familiar with scholarship in its various phases and able to decide upon the relative merits of candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: the president should be thoroughly acquainted with college routine, clear in views concerning courses of study and methods of instruction, and up in matters relating to marks, examinations, discipline, and the like. He should have high ideals but not be a doctrinaire or a dreamer. Failure in any one of these qualifications can cause overall failure. (Text examples and scoring: presence of tact, executive force, and faculty harmony are weighted heavily.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appointing solely for religious/sectarian identity
rubrics_metrics.description: A college head should not be appointed merely because he is a clergyman or of a particular denomination; appointment should be based on broader fitness and educational qualifications rather than sectarian affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the essay criticizes choosing a popular clergyman who lacked educational skill and caused institutional suffering. Religious identity may be relevant for institutions with explicit religious missions, but it should not override demonstrated educational ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer proven experience and internal progression
rubrics_metrics.description: High positions should normally be earned by faithful service and proved capacity in lower grades; the loftiest positions should be earned by demonstrated performance in related roles rather than awarded solely for success in an unrelated profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: it is safer that a president or officer rise through tutorships and professorships, showing fitness progressively. Exceptional cases are rare and should not establish general principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professor appointment: subject-matter expertise and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Professors should be chosen for special knowledge of the branch to be taught (e.g., a Latin chair requires scholarship in Latin); good character and efficiency are essential qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include appointing persons with no genuine scholarship because of favoritism, nepotism, or sectarianism. Such appointments lead to inefficiency, superficiality, and reputational decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tutor appointment: same standards as professors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tutors should be chosen for qualifications essentially the same as those demanded of professors; appointments to tutorships should be drawn from competent young scholars preparing for teaching and should allow legitimate promotion to higher posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should recruit tutors who have specialized preparation (e.g., study at leading universities) and aim to develop them for future professorships. Avoid appointing tutors without subject preparation or assigning tutors arbitrarily to unrelated subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching effectiveness expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every college teacher must 'feel' the subject, rouse students' interest, stimulate thought, encourage advanced students, and remove difficulties for strugglers; perfunctory instruction and 'teaching machines' are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly for lower college classes, scholarly vigor and enthusiasm are critical to awaken and sustain student interest. Evaluations should stress demonstrated ability to engage and educate, not merely credential presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid favoritism, nepotism, and sectarian tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments should not be determined by favoritism, nepotism, or sectarian conformity; good character and scholarship must be considered alongside competency, and sectarian questions (e.g., 'What church do you go to?') are improper bases for hiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sons of presidents being appointed without proper training, or clergy chosen to 'provide for' them despite incompetence. Such practices produce intellectual dishonesty and institutional decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match specialty to teaching assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not appoint or require faculty to teach subjects for which they lack specialized preparation; chairs should be filled by those with the relevant scholarship rather than assigning staff randomly to any subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: rules forcing faculty to teach 'any subject' under penalty of dismissal produce superficial instruction and dishonesty. Institutions should assign teaching to align with individual specialties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of appointment — avoid personal lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal lobbying (candidates and friends seeking pledges from individual trustees) is an objectionable appointment method and should not determine educational appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay calls this practice worse in education than in politics; it's an anti-pattern that corrupts the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of appointment — presidential recommendation (conditional)
rubrics_metrics.description: The president may decide between candidates and recommend an appointment; this can work if the president is wise, considers all interested parties, consults faculty associates, and weights their advice — but it risks factionalism and conflict if faculties are split.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method's success depends on the character and tact of the president. It may lead to inharmonious outcomes where faculties are cliquish or alumni/tutors exert pressure; with an old, factionalized faculty it often creates long-term trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of appointment — faculty recommendation preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment upon the unanimous or majority recommendation of the faculty is described as the most satisfactory method: it divides responsibility, reduces accusations of favoritism, and leverages the faculty's direct knowledge of educational fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Sheffield Scientific School practice (no professor called except on unanimous faculty recommendation) produced an exceptionally harmonious and efficient school. Faculty judgment is valued because members know candidates' scholarly standing and likely collegiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment procedure for newly organized schools
rubrics_metrics.description: When an institution is being organized, trustees should select a strong and competent president in whom they have full confidence and empower him (almost autocratically) to choose the initial faculty; subsequent appointments should then be referred to that faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception recognizes that a faculty does not exist yet to make recommendations. Trustees should still not surrender authority entirely; faculty recommendations should be ignored only for very substantial reasons. The initial president should assemble a coherent team that will function harmoniously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance principle: method by usage and policy, not rigid rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The method by which teachers are appointed should be a matter of usage and policy rather than a strict prescribed rule; the chosen method should promote harmony between faculty and trustees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faculty and trustees distrust each other, mischief follows. Appointment methods should be designed to produce concert of action and long-term institutional efficiency rather than short-term expedients.
